title: A Wardrobe for the Undertow
premise: Felix Underhill has spent twelve years mailing postcards to a house that no longer exists, addressed to Marisol Vane, the woman he loved and never told. When the burned house is finally demolished, a contractor's daughter, Ada Vane—Marisol's niece and executor of her fading memory—finds a box of undelivered letters hidden behind a wardrobe, including every postcard Felix ever sent. As Ada reads them to her aunt, whose dementia flickers between decades, she uncovers why the family arranged itself around silence: Marisol chose duty over Felix after her brother's death left her guardian to a child. The novel ends with Marisol's death, at which Felix is finally present; he speaks the unsaid sentence aloud at her graveside, and Ada, inheriting both the letters and the lesson, mails one last postcard—to herself, at an address she hasn't lost yet.
about_author: F. M. Okafor is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing undelivered mail in a coastal municipal records office. They write literary fiction about the objects people leave behind when they cannot leave words.

chapters.title: The Address That Burned
chapters.summary: Felix Underhill, 61, buys his weekly postcard and writes almost nothing on it. POV: Felix. We learn the ritual: twelve years of near-confessions mailed to a ruin. Emotional beat: tender absurdity—the comfort of a habit that can never be answered.

chapters.title: Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: The town posts notice: the Vane house will be razed. POV: Felix. He walks the property line at dusk, touching the fence, and learns Marisol still lives—in her niece's care across town. Emotional beat: dread disguised as relief; the last wall between him and the truth is coming down.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Ada Vane, 29, supervises the salvage crew and finds a cavity behind the bedroom wardrobe stuffed with letters—hers aunt's name on all of them, none opened. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: the vertigo of inheriting a secret you didn't ask for.

chapters.title: What Aunt Mari Kept
chapters.summary: Ada brings the box home; Marisol, sharp then foggy, calls it 'the weather from before.' POV: Ada. She recognizes Felix Underhill's handwriting from childhood Christmases. Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into protectiveness—who was this man to her family?

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Almost
chapters.summary: Ada reads the first postcards aloud while Marisol braids fringe. The early ones are funny, oblique, full of tides and weather that mean something else. POV: alternating Ada/Marisol fragments. Emotional beat: falling for a love story through its circumlocutions.

chapters.title: The Brother
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Marisol's POV, 1979: her brother Denny drowns in the undertow off Gull Point; Felix was there that day and pulled her out instead. Emotional beat: guilt as architecture—the moment the family began arranging itself around what wasn't said.

chapters.title: Duty, Worn Like Wool
chapters.summary: Marisol's flashback continues: she becomes Ada's mother's guardian figure, takes over the family shop, lets Felix sail away without answering his one direct letter. POV: Marisol. Emotional beat: love renounced with such competence it looks like choice.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Counter
chapters.summary: Ada tracks Felix to the stationery shop where he works. She doesn't reveal the box; she buys a postcard and watches him write nothing. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: recognition—she is looking at a man mid-sentence, forty years long.

chapters.title: The Family Arrangement
chapters.summary: Ada's mother, Ruth, arrives to 'help' and demands the box be sealed or burned; the family's peace, she says, depends on it. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: the machinery of silence revealed—not cruelty, but a load-bearing lie.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud
chapters.summary: Ada defies Ruth and reads the middle years' postcards to Marisol, who surfaces briefly and finishes one from memory, word for word. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness—Marisol kept every word even as she lost the world.

chapters.title: Undertow
chapters.summary: Marisol's flashback: the summer after Denny's death, she and Felix nearly speak at Gull Point; the sea takes her words again. POV: Marisol. Emotional beat: grief as undertow—it doesn't pull you out, it pulls everything you try to say under.

chapters.title: Ruth's Version
chapters.summary: Ruth tells Ada her own story: she grew up watching her mother choose a ghost over the living, and swore the household would not drown twice. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: sympathy for the jailer; silence as inheritance, fiercely given.

chapters.title: The Unsent One
chapters.summary: At the bottom of the box, Ada finds a letter Marisol wrote to Felix and never sent—dated three weeks ago, lucid, asking him to come before she forgets how to want him to. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: the ground shifts; the secret was mutual, and recent.

chapters.title: Time Already Running Out
chapters.summary: Marisol declines sharply—a fall, a hospital night, longer fogs. Doctors recommend hospice at home. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: urgency compressing every moral question into days.

chapters.title: Delivering It Herself
chapters.summary: Ada hand-delivers Marisol's letter to Felix's shop and waits while he reads it standing up. POV: Felix. He says only, 'Which door do I knock on?' Emotional beat: twelve years ending in logistics; love reduced to an address, finally correct.

chapters.title: The House Before the House Falls
chapters.summary: Felix visits; Marisol, in a clear hour, greets him by the nickname only Denny used. They sit with the wardrobe salvaged from the demolition, empty now. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: reunion without resolution—two people fluent in almost.

chapters.title: Ruth at the Door
chapters.summary: Ruth arrives to find Felix's coat on the chair and orders him out; Marisol, suddenly fierce, says the sentence she's rehearsed forty years: 'I chose wrong, and I'm done paying.' POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: the arrangement collapses; grief and liberation in one breath.

chapters.title: Climax: What the Tide Takes
chapters.summary: Marisol's final lucid evening: she asks Felix to read her own unsent letter back to her so she can hear herself say it once. He does; she answers 'yes' to a question asked decades late. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: climax—the art of almost saying it ends in saying it.

chapters.title: The Quiet After
chapters.summary: Marisol dies two mornings later, holding Felix's hand, Ada on the bed's other side, Ruth in the doorway choosing to stay. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: sorrow without regret—the rarest kind.

chapters.title: Graveside
chapters.summary: At the burial, Felix speaks the sentence whole—the one the postcards circled for twelve years—and the family hears it as eulogy rather than scandal. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: justice outside the law; the truth spoken too late and exactly on time.

chapters.title: Inheritance
chapters.summary: Ada sorts the estate: she keeps the wardrobe, gives Ruth the shop ledger, and finds Marisol's will leaves her 'the box and the obligation to answer my mail.' POV: Ada. Emotional beat: weight transformed into instruction.

chapters.title: A Postcard to Myself
chapters.summary: Ada writes a postcard to her own current address—something true she's been circling about a woman named June—and drops it in the slot, trusting tomorrow's delivery. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: resolution; the cycle broken not by silence but by sending it while you still can.
